reverse_outline.summary: Scope of the part: supply's path from arrival to visibility and removal, chapter topics listed
Business stake: professional feeds drive inventory and paid leads, so supply failures cost renewals
Architect stake: supply is where outside systems write in, so its weaknesses spread downstream

Three key points: one write path with a contract per channel / provenance-preserving normalization and entity resolution / publication and removal propagated within time budgets, checked by professionals
Failure patterns the part fixes: feed roulette, duplicate listings, ghost inventory
Transition from Part II's listing model to supply arriving through many uncontrolled channels
Thesis that supply is one chain of links, and a roadmap of the rest of the part
Table of chapters in chain order with each one's question and triggering symptom
Dependencies on other parts: consumes Part II contracts, targets from Part I metrics, moderation from Part V
The fictional Veldmark team's supply incidents and fixes across the chapters
Recap of the chain, why Part IV depends on it, and pointer to the first chapter

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

Outline 'Transition from Part II's listing model to supply arriving through many uncontrolled channels' matches the controlling idea (Part II's model put under load by many doors). Same order as the spec.
Outline 'Thesis that supply is one chain of links, and a roadmap of the rest of the part' matches the claim plus the order of chapters and what follows. Same order as the spec.
Outline 'Table of chapters in chain order with each one's question and triggering symptom' matches. Same order as the spec.
Outline 'consumes Part II contracts, targets from Part I metrics, moderation from Part V' matches all three parts of the controlling idea. Same order as the spec.
Outline 'Veldmark team's supply incidents and fixes across the chapters' matches incidents answered one per chapter. Same order as the spec.
Outline 'Recap of the chain, why Part IV depends on it, and pointer to the first chapter' matches synthesis, so-what and hand-off. Same order as the spec.

The outliner marked the KEY POINTS callout as more than one idea; it is the house-format three-bullet callout that the spec places the part's claim in (one chain, its links in three bullets), so several bullets are by design. No prose unit was marked.
Sets up the problem the thesis answers (many doors, each its own idea of a listing).
States the thesis and the chapter order (PIII-1).
Supports PIII-1: chapters in chain order, each with a symptom.
Supports PIII-2: what the chain consumes from Parts I and II, and the Part V gate.
Supports PIII-3: one Veldmark incident or mismatch per chapter, in chapter order.
Synthesizes the thesis and gives its so-what (Part IV inherits the chain).
The many-doors example is followed by its point: each door grows its own idea of a listing.
Figure 1 follows the thesis it illustrates and its caption states what it shows: every door feeds the same contracted path, which also takes listings down.
The lead-in says the rows are in chain order and give each chapter's question and the symptom that sends you there; AC-2's reader used the table exactly so.

The lead-in ('supply problems arrive as incidents before designs') states what the five bullets show. The added, unexplained clauses in two bullets are recorded under known_before_new and flow_is_followable.
Problem→solution: 'The argument is that supply is one chain' answers the many doors of ¶1.
Elaboration: 'In chain order, each row gives a chapter's question…' unfolds the links just listed.

results.quote: Last, the professionals check the result, down to lead counts, against their own systems.
results.finding: Both flow readers stopped here: the fifth chapter's subject is appended to a bullet headed 'Publishing is a decision followed by a propagation, and removal matters more', which does not cover it, so it reads as an afterthought rather than the chain's last link. The spec's order (professional check as last link) is fine; the bullet's heading and wording obscure it.

results.quote: using only what each listing carries as published to Hearthly, never data from Keybridge, the group's agency software that also feeds rival portals: agencies fear Veldmark would use their data to favor Hearthly.
results.finding: Both flow readers had to re-read the Lyon bullet: a rule, a negation, a gloss and the reason after a colon are stacked in one sentence, and Hearthly is the only brand on the page left unglossed while the others are. The content is the spec's; the sentence construction obscures it.

results.quote: and keeps Keybridge's cross-portal report out of Hearthly's reach.
results.finding: Both flow readers found this clause out of place: it jumps from the Golf's Motorvane leads to Keybridge and Hearthly inside one bullet, and 'cross-portal report' is never explained. The spec's evidence for this bullet is the 23-versus-14 lead reconciliation only; the clause is an addition the spec does not ask for.

results.quote: by adopting **Supply Contract v1** in September 2027: one envelope, one error catalog, mandatory mass-change guards and brand-local adapters.
results.finding: Both flow readers re-read the first bullet: incident, date, brand, count, contract name and a four-item component list in one sentence. The spec's evidence names only the incident and Supply Contract v1; the component list is added density.

results.quote: The last link is the professionals' check of its output against their own systems.
results.finding: One flow reader re-read this: professionals were just presented as a door supply enters through, now they are the chain's last link, and 'its output' has a loose referent. Single reader; recorded as minor.

results.finding: 'Mass-change guard' is on the spec's does_not_know list (owned by listing-ingestion) and the page uses it without giving it; 'brand-local adapters' is likewise unexplained. Both flow readers reported these terms as unexplained. The spec's evidence does not require the component list.

results.finding: Opens with a bridge from Part II and a direct statement of the problem, then the thesis and a roadmap; no placeholder, restated question, dictionary, dawn-of-man or book-report opening.
Synthesis, a so-what (Part IV) and a course of action; no new subtopic, no 'in conclusion' opener, no body evidence, not a bare rephrase of the thesis.

'a contract per door, a source for every value, a removal that reaches every copy' synthesizes the links; Part IV's dependence on the chain answers so-what; 'Begin with [[listing-ingestion]]' gives the takeaway (the spec's alternative of opening the table's chapter is implicit from the table).
'turn many doors into one chain' names what p01's many doors become.

The cold reader predicted the table, the part's place in the book and the Veldmark thread in that order, and named the five chapters in order: ingestion under per-channel contracts for forms, APIs and feeds; normalization and enrichment with recorded sources; entity resolution of several listings of one thing; publication and removal within a time budget; professional tooling as the professionals' check of the output. It was least sure how far chapter 5 goes beyond reconciliation, but named its subject; this matches AC-1's expected answer.
The reader chose listing-ingestion for the bad file and professional-seller-tooling for the disputed lead counts, as expected.
